title: Probability and statistical inference · Rung 1
subtitle: Probability, random variables, and the difference between a parameter and an estimate
coverLine: Why a positive test usually means less than it seems, and what a reported number is a number of
subject: S03
author: Dr. Harsh Maheshwari

about.why: A positive test result usually feels like an answer. Often it is not, and most doctors asked to work out what it means give a number far too high. This book teaches the rules of probability that settle the question, ending at Bayes’ theorem, and the handful of patterns of chance that keep turning up in health data. Then it separates three things a reported number can be: a fact about everyone, an estimate from a sample, or a prediction. Every later book on statistics leans on these ideas, and so does every conversation with a patient about a test.
about.howToRead: Read Book 0 and Book 2 first, or at least the sections this book names as it goes. Then read this one in order, with a pen and a calculator, and do the practice problems in each section before you read on. The book asks you to build one thing: a one-page handout explaining a positive result for a test used in your own clinic. Choose the test and find your clinic’s register before you start, because one section asks you to count how common the condition is among your own patients.
about.prerequisites: Book 0, in particular percentages (A4), ratios and proportions (A5), powers and roots (A6), and all of Part D: what a probability is and odds (D1), independence (D2), the two-way table with sensitivity, specificity and the positive predictive value (D3), mean and standard deviation (D5) and parameter against statistic (D6). Book 2, sections 1, 4 and 13 to 15: the symbols and the Σ sign (1), e and natural logarithms (4), and the random variable, expectation and variance (13 to 15). The mathematics is arithmetic with a calculator, fractions, powers, the sum sign, and one-line algebra; no calculus is needed beyond reading an area under a curve as a probability, which Book 2 taught.

blurb: A short book on probability for people who order tests and read research. It covers the rules every probability obeys, conditional probability and independence, Bayes' theorem worked first by counting people and then by formula, and why most clinicians misjudge a positive result. It teaches the binomial, Poisson and normal patterns and what produces each, covariance, and what happens when you average many draws. It ends by separating a parameter from an estimate and a prediction, and with a handout on a real test, for your own clinic.
